reconcile.connective: Defenders resolve Anah's shifting identity textually, following the Samaritan, Septuagint, and Syriac that read "son" for the Masoretic "daughter" in Genesis 36:2, 14.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells presses the plain Masoretic text, where Anah is at once Zibeon's daughter, Zibeon's son, and Seir's son — making Zibeon both Anah's father and brother.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Who was Anah?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/anah.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "Who was Anah?" (2013)

excerpts.excerpt_text: But this same Anah is said to be the son of Zibeon, Gen 36:24, though in this and Gen 36:14 he is said to be the daughter of Zibeon. But the Samaritan, the Septuagint, (and the Syriac, in Gen 36:2), read son instead of daughter, which Houbigant and Kennicott contend to be the true reading.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly states the son-vs-daughter-of-Zibeon conflict across Gen 36:2/14/24 and offers the textual-variant harmonization (Sam/LXX/Syriac 'son'). Two adjacent verbatim sentences, both ending on real source periods. Strongest single reconcile; parity-capped to 1 against the discrepancy pole's lone named-skeptic count.

pd_work.note: Clarke treats the Anah identity contradiction directly, resolving the son/daughter conflict via the Samaritan, Septuagint, and Syriac reading of 'son' (Haley's specific coverage of this pair unconfirmed; row-surfaced harmonizing commentator keyed to the passage per spec).
